The answer depends on which review and which comparison you mean, because none of the reviews gives a single "number of cathodes compared." Counted figure by figure and table by table:

**1. aenm-2022 (Co-free cathodes review)**
- **Cost and cobalt/nickel model, Figure 2:** 10 cathodes (p. 3).
  - Five contain cobalt: NMC333, NMC532, NMC622, NMC811 and NCA.
  - Five are "zero cobalt": NFA, NMA, NA91, NM91 and LiNiO₂.
  - The text introducing this model names only a subset: NMC111, NMC622, NCA, LiNiO₂, NMA and NFA (p. 2).
- **Potential/capacity/specific-energy map, Figure 3b:** 6 mainstream cathodes: LCO, NCA, NMC, LMO, LNMO and LFP (p. 4).
- **Smaller comparisons:**
  - Five Mn-substituted LNO compositions, LiNi₀.₉Mn₀.₁O₂ through LiNi₀.₅Mn₀.₅O₂ (Fig. 4, p. 5).
  - LNO and Al-, Mn-, Mg- and Co-doped LNO, set against commercial NCA (Fig. 5, pp. 4–6).
  - Four Co-free ternary cathodes: NM82, NMT, NMM and NMA (Fig. 7, p. 8).
  - Four DRX cathodes (Fig. 9, p. 11).

**2. ensm-2021 (surface-coatings review)**
- **Table 4:** 23 coated-versus-uncoated cathode comparisons, grouped by coating class (p. 13):
  - 8 oxides
  - 4 phosphates
  - 4 ionic conductors
  - 3 electrode-material coatings
  - 4 conductive polymers
- Several base cathodes repeat across these rows, notably NCM811 and Li₁.₂Ni₀.₁₃Mn₀.₅₄Co₀.₁₃O₂.

**3. mattod-2020 (recycling review)**
- It does not compare cathode performance.
- It lists five cathode chemistries that complicate recycling: LCO, NMC, LFP, NCA and LMO (p. 3).
- Its Figure 2 compares the composition of an NMC622 Li-ion cell with a lead-acid battery (p. 3).

If you meant one specific review or figure, tell me which and I can narrow this down.
